en: The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra in Four Divisions,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin Dynasty.
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, As well as to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya teachings, so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The precepts are like a boundless ocean; like jewels, they are sought without satiety.
Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, assemble and listen as I speak.
To eliminate the eight *pārājika* rules, and to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules,
as well as the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses— assemble, O assembly,
and listen as I speak. Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, [Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa].
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni—these World-Honored Ones of great virtue have explained this matter for me.
Now I wish to explain it well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts:
they cannot be reborn among gods or humans. If one wishes to be born in the heavens or as a human being, [one must maintain the precepts].
One should always protect the feet of the precepts, never allowing them to be damaged.
Just as a driver entering a perilous path fears the loss of a pin or the breaking of an axle, so it is with the violation of the precepts;
at the time of death, one will harbor fear and dread.
Just as a person looking into a mirror feels joy or grief at their own beauty or ugliness, so it is with the recitation of the precepts:
one feels sorrow or delight based on whether they are fully observed or violated.
It is like two armies fighting together, where the brave advance and the timid retreat.
The recitation of the precepts is likewise: from purity comes peace, from defilement comes fear.
Among worldly beings, the king is supreme; among all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme;
among the stars, the moon is supreme; and among all holy ones, the Buddha is supreme.
Among all the various codes of discipline, the Sūtra of Precepts is supreme;
the Tathāgata established these prohibitions and recites them every half-month.
"Has the Saṃgha assembled?"
He replied, "The Sangha has assembled.
[The other asked,] "Are you in harmony?"
He replied, "The assembly is in harmony.
[The Buddha asked,] "Let those who have not yet received the full ordination depart?"
If there is someone present, he should be sent out.
Once he has been sent out, [the monk] replies:
"He has been sent out."
When asked, "Are there none? she replied, "There are none.
[He asked again,] "Did no bhikṣuṇīs who did not come state their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*?"
If it exists, speak according to the Dharma;
if it does not exist, answer:
"It does not exist."
“The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it do?
He replied, “We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts.”
“Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day, and the community of monks shall recite the precepts.
If the time has come for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let us recite the precepts in harmony.”
"The announcement has been made thus. "Has the announcement been completed? He replied:
“It is settled. Sisters,
I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.”
Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect upon this well.
If you know that you have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it;
those who have not committed an offense should remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that the elder sisters are pure.
If anyone else asks, they should answer in the same way.
Thus, if a bhikṣuṇī remains in the assembly and, after being questioned up to three times, remembers having committed an offense but does not confess it, she incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Therefore, the Buddha has declared that false speech is a dharma that obstructs the path.
If a bhikṣuṇī remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purification, she should perform confession.
Confession brings peace and happiness.
Sisters! I have now recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
"Now I ask the sisters:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus, up to three times."
"Sisters! You are pure in this matter, for you remain silent.
Thus shall this matter be upheld."
"Sisters! These eight *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
'If a bhikṣuṇī commits sexual intercourse, an impure act, even with an animal.'"
This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind;
according to the object stolen, if she is seized by a king or a royal minister, or is bound, or killed, or driven out of the country: [she commits a pārājika offense]."
"You thief! You fool!
You know nothing!"
If a bhikṣuṇī commits such taking of what is not given, this bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in community.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of a human being with her own hand, or provides a weapon to another, or praises death, extols death, or encourages death, saying: 'Ho! [Why do you live?
It would be better to die!]'..."
"What use is this miserable life?
It would be better to die than to live.
With such thoughts, he used countless skillful means to lament death, praise death, and exhort others toward death.
This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while having no actual knowledge, praises herself, saying:
'I have attained a state beyond the human, I have entered the noble wisdom and supreme dharma; I know this, I see this.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, desiring to seek purity, she speaks thus: "Sisters!
I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said that I knew and I saw; this was empty, deceptive, and false speech."
"Excepting those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
this bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion.
'If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, makes physical contact below the armpits and above the knees with a man who has a defiled mind.'"
Whether grasping or rubbing, whether pulling or pushing, whether stroking upward or stroking downward, whether lifting up or lowering down, whether seizing or pressing down.
This bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in communion.
This refers to physical contact.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, knowing that a man has a defiled mind, accepts his taking her hand, taking her robe, entering a secluded place, standing together, speaking together, walking together, or leaning their bodies against one another, or makes an appointment [to meet]."
This bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in community.
This is because she has committed these eight offenses:
"If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense, yet does not disclose it herself, does not inform others, and does not report it to the Saṃgha."
If, at another time, that bhikṣuṇī has either passed away, been censured by the community, left the religious life, or joined a group of external sects, and later says:
"I previously knew that I had such and such an offense."
"Such a bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in communion.
This is because she concealed a grave offense.

'If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally censured by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, yet he does not comply, does not repent, and the Saṃgha has not yet granted him communion;..."
She followed their instructions obediently.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Sister!..."

This bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; yet he does not comply and does not repent, and the Saṃgha has not yet granted him communal residence.
You must not comply with him.
When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished that bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter],
those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time, in order to cause her to relinquish this matter.
Up to three admonitions, if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in community;
this is because she has committed an offense subject to formal censure.
"Sisters! I have now recited the eight *pārājika* dharmas.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these *pārājika* dharmas, she may not dwell together with the bhikṣuṇīs as she did before, nor may she do so thereafter. This bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community."
"Now I ask the sisters:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus, up to three times: 'Sisters!'"
In this matter, we are pure, for we remain silent.
Thus shall this be upheld. "Sisters!..."
These seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a go-between, conveying a man’s words to a woman and conveying a woman’s words to a man."

If, for the purpose of consummating marriage or for the purpose of illicit intercourse, even for a mere moment, this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished: a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *pārājika* offense, wishing to destroy that person's pure conduct;
and later, whether she is questioned or not, it is found that the matter was groundless and she says:
'I spoke thus because I was angry.'"
This bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished, a saṃghāvaśeṣa:

“If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, takes up a fragment from a matter belonging to a different category and, though the bhikṣuṇī is not one who has committed a pārājika offense, she slanders her with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy that person’s brahmacarya.”
Later, at another time, whether questioned or unasked, it was known that she had taken a portion from matters belonging to a different category;
that bhikṣuṇī, dwelling in a state of anger, made such a statement.
This nun has committed an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a nun goes to an official and speaks of a layperson, or the son of a layperson, or a slave, or a hired laborer—whether by day or by night, for even the duration of a single thought-moment, a finger-snap, or a brief instant."
This nun has committed an offense involving the initial rule that must be relinquished; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a nun, knowing beforehand that a woman is a thief whose crime deserves death and is known to the public, ordains her as a renunciant and grants her full ordination (*upasampadā*) without having inquired of the king, a high minister, or her lineage—"
This nun has committed an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a nun, knowing that another nun has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, yet does not comply, has not confessed her fault, and the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for her reinstatement;
out of affection, and without having consulted the Saṃgha or received its authorization, she goes outside the boundary and performs a formal act to absolve her of the offense."
This nun has committed an offense requiring confession and renunciation; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a nun crosses a body of water alone, enters a village alone, stays overnight alone, or walks behind alone."
This nun has committed an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, knowing a man to have a defiled mind, receives from him edible food, staple food, or other items."
This nun has committed an offense requiring the initial forfeiture; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a nun instructs another nun to speak as follows: 'Sister!'"
Whether he possesses a defiled mind or is free from a defiled mind, what can that do to you?
As for yourself, being free from a defiled mind, if you receive food from him at the proper time, accept it with purity.
This nun has committed an offense involving the first rule that must be relinquished; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a nun, wishing to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, diligently employs skillful means to adopt the methods for breaking the Saṃgha and persists in holding to them without relinquishing them..."
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept the dharma of schism and persistently hold to it without relinquishing it."
"Sister! You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

Being in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and not disputing, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk blending together, you will find increase in the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness."
When that bhikṣuṇī admonishes the other bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish the matter,
that bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times so that she may abandon this course of action.
Up to three admonitions, it is well if she relinquishes [the offense].
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī commits a third offense that must be relinquished; it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa, number ten.
"If a bhikṣuṇī has a faction of other bhikṣuṇīs— whether one, two, three, or even countless—
those bhikṣuṇīs say to that bhikṣuṇī: 'Sister!'"
"Do not admonish this bhikṣuṇī; this bhikṣuṇī is one who speaks according to the Dharma, one who speaks according to the Vinaya.
What this bhikṣuṇī says, we delight in with our hearts;
what this bhikṣuṇī says, we accept."
That bhikṣuṇī said to the other bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Do not speak in this way!"
They said:
"This bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Dharma; this bhikṣuṇī speaks according to the Vinaya.
What this bhikṣuṇī has spoken, we delight in."
"What this bhikṣuṇī has said, we accept and approve.
Why is that? What this bhikṣuṇī has said is not a discourse on the Dharma, nor is it a discourse on the Vinaya.
Sister! Do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha; rather, you should desire harmony within the Saṃgha, Sister!

Being in harmony with the Sangha, rejoicing without contention, and studying under the same teacher as one water merging with milk, you shall find increase in the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness.
When that bhikṣuṇī admonishes the other bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish the matter,
the former bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times so that she may abandon this course of action.
Up to three admonitions, it is well if she relinquishes [the behavior].
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that must be relinquished.
"If a bhikṣuṇī dwells in dependence upon a city or a village, defiles a family, and engages in evil conduct..."
"She has been seen and heard to engage in evil conduct;
she has been seen and heard to defile families.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! You defile families and engage in evil conduct.
That you engage in evil conduct is both seen and heard."
"You defile the families of others; this we both see and hear. Sister!
You have defiled the families and practiced evil conduct; you should now depart from this village and need not remain here."
That bhikṣuṇī said this to the other bhikṣuṇī: "Sister!
The bhikṣuṇīs have favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion; for bhikṣuṇīs who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not."
Those bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Do not speak such words."
"There is attachment, there is aversion, there is fear, and there is delusion.
Nor should one say: "There are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not."
Why is this? Because these bhikṣuṇīs are not motivated by attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion; thus, among bhikṣuṇīs who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not.
"Sister! You have defiled families and committed evil deeds.
That you commit evil deeds is both seen and heard."
"She defiles the families of others; this we have both seen and heard.

When that bhikṣuṇī admonishes the other bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish the matter, that bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times so that she may abandon this course of action.
Up to three admonitions, it is well if she relinquishes [the offense].
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense involving three factors that must be relinquished.

"If a bhikṣuṇī is of an evil nature and will not accept the words of others, and after the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in accordance with the Dharma regarding the precepts, she herself does not accept the words of admonition, saying:..."
"Sisters! Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you of what is good or bad.
Sisters, please desist!"
"Do not admonish me.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister!..."
Do not, sister, refuse to accept admonition for yourself;
you should, sister,
accept admonition for yourself.
"Sister, you should admonish the bhikṣuṇīs in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣuṇīs should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples attains growth through mutual admonition, mutual instruction, and mutual confession."
When this bhikṣuṇī is thus admonished and persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter],
that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished up to three times so that she may abandon this course of action.
If she abandons it by the third admonition, it is well.
Regarding "not relinquishing": if a bhikṣuṇī commits these three offenses which ought to be relinquished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī lives in close association with another, they engage in evil conduct together, their ill repute spreads abroad, and they repeatedly conceal each other's offenses."
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish those bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "Sisters!
You must not associate with one another, engage in evil conduct together, spread an evil reputation, or conceal each other's offenses."
"If you do not associate with one another, you will attain increase and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.
When that bhikṣuṇī admonished her, the other bhikṣuṇī persisted and would not relinquish her position.
This bhikṣuṇī should be admonished three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving three matters that must be relinquished, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"If, when the Saṃgha is formally reprimanding and admonishing a bhikṣuṇī, other bhikṣuṇīs instruct her, saying:
'Do not live separately; you should live together!'"
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs who did not live separately, yet engaged in evil conduct together, whose ill repute spread abroad, and who concealed their offenses from one another.
Out of anger, the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately.
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not instruct other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:..."
"Do not live separately; I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, committing evil deeds together, spreading an evil reputation, and covering for one another's offenses."
"Because of their anger, the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately.
Now it is precisely these two bhikṣuṇīs who are living together, committing evil deeds, spreading an evil reputation, and covering for one another's offenses; there are no others besides them.
"If this bhikṣuṇī lives separately, there will be increase and peaceful dwelling within the Buddha-dharma.
When these bhikṣuṇīs admonish that bhikṣuṇī, she stubbornly maintains her position and does not relinquish it.
This bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving three matters that must be relinquished, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure over even a minor matter, should speak thus:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha.'"
"It is not only these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; there are also other śramaṇas and brahmins who practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and we too may practice the holy life under them."
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!
Do not, on account of a mere trifle, become angry and displeased, and then speak these words:..."
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, and I renounce the Saṅgha.
It is not only these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who exist; there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life."
"We too may practice the holy life there. If,
when these bhikṣuṇīs are admonishing that bhikṣuṇī, she persists and does not relinquish her position,
those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
Up to three times he should be admonished; if she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense involving three points that must be relinquished.
"If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and does not properly remember the matter of the dispute, and later, out of anger, speaks these words:..."
"The Saṃgha has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister!..."
Do not delight in quarreling, nor harbor ill-will regarding the matter of the dispute; later, out of anger, do not speak these words:
"The Saṃgha has favoritism, it has hatred, it has fear, and it has delusion."
"The Saṃgha is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion;
it is you who possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
When this bhikṣuṇī thus exhorts that other bhikṣuṇī, she persists in her position and does not relinquish it.
That bhikṣuṇī should be admonished three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which involves three factors and must be relinquished.
"Venerable sisters!
I have now recited the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine offenses that constitute a crime upon commission, and eight that require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these offenses, she must undergo *mānatva* for half a month before both divisions of the Saṃgha."

Once the *mānatva* has been performed, there remains the matter of the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*). This nun’s offense must be removed before an assembly of the two divisions consisting of forty monks.
If there is one person short and the assembly does not number forty, the nun’s offense cannot be removed, and the nuns may also censure them.
This is the proper time.
Now I ask the sisters:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it was repeated a second and a third time: “Sisters,
you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent.”
This matter is to be upheld in this way. "Sisters,
these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, keeps an extra robe for ten days without having performed the 'unclean' distribution (aśuddha-dāna), she may retain it."
If she exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished making her robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* privileges, should stay overnight apart from any one of her five robes in a different location for even a single night—unless there has been a formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) by the Saṃgha—it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, should obtain an out-of-season robe, she may accept it if she needs it; having accepted it, she must quickly have it made into a robe."
If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is insufficient, one may keep it for one month in order to fulfill the requirement.
If one keeps it beyond that period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
Regarding the "proper time" herein:
if one’s robes have been taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water, this is called the proper time.

If a bhikṣuṇī’s robes have been taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites her at her own discretion and offers many robes, that bhikṣuṇī should accept the robes with contentment.
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a householder or a householder’s wife provides the price for a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'With this amount of robe-price, provide a robe for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. "
If this bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation for a formal invitation (pravāraṇā), goes to the house of a layperson and speaks thus:
"Excellent, layperson!
Prepare such and such a price for a robe for me and give it to me."
If, for the sake of desiring something fine, she should obtain a robe [with that money], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If two laymen or two laywomen provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'We have provided the price for such a robe to give to a certain bhikṣuṇī.'"
"Before having received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, this bhikṣuṇī went to the houses of two lay devotees and spoke thus:
'Excellent, lay devotees!'"
"Having prepared such and such a price for robes, let us together make one robe.
If, for the sake of obtaining something fine, she obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having been sent a messenger by a king, a high official, a brahmin, a householder, or a householder’s wife, to deliver the price for robes with the instruction:
'Take this price for robes and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī'..."
That messenger went to where the bhikṣuṇī was and said:
"Ayyā! I have brought the price for your robe; please accept it."
That bhikṣuṇī should speak to that messenger as follows:
"I ought not to accept this price for a robe; if I require a robe, I shall accept one that is timely and pure."
The messenger said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Ayye! Is there anyone who manages affairs for you?"
The bhikṣuṇī who needs robes said: "There are!
Whether they be monastery attendants or upāsakas, these are the attendants for the bhikṣuṇīs, who constantly perform services for them."
That messenger, having gone to the person in charge and delivered the price for the robe, returned to the bhikṣuṇī and spoke thus:
"Venerable lady!
I have already given the price for the robe to the person in charge whom you indicated."
"Sister!
Know the time; go there and you shall obtain the robe.
If a bhikṣuṇī requires a robe, she should go to the place where the attendant is and speak these words two or three times:
"I need a robe.
If he succeeds in obtaining a robe after reminding him thus two or three times, that is well.
If he does not obtain a robe, he should stand silently before him for four, five, or six times to cause him to remember.
If he stands silently before [the donor] four, five, or six times, it is well if he obtains the robe.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain it beyond that number of times, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should go to the place from which the messenger came, either going herself or sending a messenger, and say:
"The robe-price you previously sent by messenger to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī was not obtained by that bhikṣuṇī at all."
“Take this back; do not let it be lost—this is the proper time.
“If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes gold, silver, or money, or causes another to take them, or accepts them by word of mouth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of trade and commerce, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī has an alms bowl with fewer than five mends that is not leaking, yet she seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

This bhikṣuṇī must take this bowl and relinquish it before the community of bhikṣuṇīs. It shall be traded down through the ranks until it reaches the lowest-ranking nun; the bowl of that lowest-ranking nun is then given to this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'Sister!'"
"Carry this bowl until it breaks; this is the proper time.
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself seeks thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe for her, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when a householder or a householder’s wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for her, and that bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation of her own accord, goes to that place and says to the weaver:
'Weave this robe for me; weave it very well, making it wide, long, firm, fine, and perfectly neat; I shall give you a small amount of payment.'"
“If a bhikṣuṇī gives a price, even for a single meal, and obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having given a robe to another bhikṣuṇī, later becomes angry and either takes it back herself or instructs another to take it away, saying:
‘Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.’”
That bhikṣuṇī should return the robe;
if she takes the robe back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If various sick bhikṣuṇīs keep medicine:..."
Regarding ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar: one may consume these leftovers from overnight storage, and may even take them for up to seven days.
If one consumes them beyond seven days, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when less than ten days remain before the end of the three-month summer retreat, receives an urgent gift of robes (ātyayika-cīvara), and the bhikṣuṇī knows it to be an urgent gift of robes, she should accept it;
having accepted it, she may keep it until the time for robes."
If she keeps it beyond that time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, seeks to have it enter her own possession, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having sought this, seeks that instead, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor’s gift intended for the Saṃgha is for one specific purpose, diverts it for another use, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for whom a gift was intended for a specific purpose, seeks it for herself or for the Saṃgha, and then diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes an item given by a donor for one purpose and diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes an item given by a donor for one purpose and, having requested it herself for the sake of the Saṃgha, diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps many vessels of fine color, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī promises a sick robe to another bhikṣuṇī and later does not give it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī accepts a non-seasonal robe and treats it as a seasonal robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having exchanged robes with another bhikṣuṇī, later becomes angry and takes them back herself, or causes someone else to take them, saying:
'Sister!'"
If one says, "Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
Your robe belongs to you, but my robe must be returned to me," it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests a heavy robe, its value shall not exceed four *kārṣāpaṇas* of cotton cloth.
Should it exceed this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to request a light robe, the maximum value shall be two and a half *kārṣāpaṇas* of cotton cloth."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. "Sisters,
I have now recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas."
"Now I ask the sisters:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus, [the question is asked] up to three times."
"Sisters! You are pure in this matter, for you remain silent.
Thus shall this matter be upheld."
"Sisters! These one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.
'If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally speaks a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
“If a bhikṣuṇī speaks disparagingly, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī engages in double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays in the same room as an unordained woman for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī recites the Dharma together with one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to a person who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to a person who has not received full ordination, saying:
'I know this; I have seen this as real,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, except when a woman of intelligence is present, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth herself or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks falsely or uses evasive speech to annoy others, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī reviles another in a contemptuous manner, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes a monastic corded bed, a wooden bed, bedding, or a sitting mat, spreads it out on open ground herself or instructs another to spread it;
and then departs without either putting it away herself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastic dwelling, takes bedding belonging to the Saṃgha and spreads it herself or instructs another to spread it, and then sits or lies upon it;
if she departs from that place without putting it away herself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has already been residing in a place, later comes and forcibly spreads out bedding in the middle to stay overnight, thinking:
'If she finds it cramped, she will naturally avoid me and leave.'"
By acting as a cause for such [an offense], and not otherwise, nor through mere decorum, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger toward another bhikṣuṇī and being displeased with her, personally drags her out of the communal monastery quarters, or instructs another to drag her out, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while on an upper story, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains insects, uses it herself to sprinkle on mud, grass, or straw, or instructs another to do so, she commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī constructs a large dwelling, the doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, as well as the instructions for the roofing and thatching, shall be limited to two or three layers."
If one exceeds [this limit], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at a place where a single meal is offered, should eat only one meal when she is not ill; if she accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats apart from the community, except at other times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).

'Other times' are: when ill, when making robes, when robes are being offered, when traveling on a road, when on a boat, during a great assembly, and when food is being offered by śramaṇas; these are the [permitted] times."

"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a donor and is earnestly invited to accept cakes or parched grain, and the bhikṣuṇī wishes to receive them, she may accept two or three bowls. She should then carry them to the monastery and distribute them among the other bhikṣuṇīs for them to eat."
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, receives more than three bowls of food and carries it back to the monastery without distributing some to other bhikṣuṇīs for them to eat, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī consumes food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, except for water and tooth-sticks, receives food or medicine and places it in her mouth without having formally accepted it, she commits a pāyattika offense.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after a meal without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, except during other [permissible] times, she commits a pāyattika offense."
The exceptions are:
when one is ill, when making robes, or when robes are being offered; these are the proper occasions.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits down forcibly in a household where there is wealth present while they are eating, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place within a household where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits alone with a man in one place on open ground, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Sister! Come with me to the village; I shall give you food.'"
That bhikṣuṇī ultimately did not give any food to this bhikṣuṇī, but spoke to her thus:
"Sister, go away!
I do not enjoy sitting or speaking with you in one place; I enjoy sitting and speaking alone."
"For this reason, and no other, if she dismisses her by means of a stratagem, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī provides medicine for four months, a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill should accept it."
If she accepts an invitation beyond the limit—except for regular invitations, repeated invitations, invitations to specific portions, or lifelong invitations—it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view an army formation, except when there is a specific reason, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī has a reason to go into an army camp, she may stay for two or three nights.
Should she exceed this, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣuṇī stays in an army camp for two or three nights, and at any time observes the military formations and combat, or observes the strength of the marching troops, elephants, and horses, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī drinks intoxicants, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī tickles one another with her fingers, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī intimidates another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī bathes every half-month, she should accept [bathing oil] only if she is not ill.
If she accepts it beyond that limit, except during other permitted times, it is a pāyattika offense."
"Other times" refers to:
the time of heat, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of high winds, the time of rain, and the time of coming from or going on a long journey; these are the [permissible] times.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being without illness, lights a fire on open ground for the sake of warming her body, or instructs another to light one, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī hides another bhikṣuṇī’s bowl, robe, sitting mat, or needle case—whether she hides it herself or instructs another to hide it—even if done in jest, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having given a robe as a pure gift (niḥśraya-dāna) to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī, subsequently takes it back and wears it without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she must dye it one of three kinds of discolored colors:
blue, black, or madder.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe and does not dye it one of these three kinds of discolored colors..."
If a nun wears a new robe that is blue, black, or madder-colored, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains insects, drinks or uses it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally harasses another bhikṣuṇī, even to the extent of causing her a moment of unhappiness, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it, she commits a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a matter of dispute within the Saṃgha has already been settled according to the Dharma through confession, subsequently raises it again, she commits a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that they are traveling companions of thieves, travels along the same road with them for even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus:
'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not a dharma that obstructs the Path.'"
Those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the World-Honored One. It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One does not speak such words."

“The World-Honored One has, by means of countless skillful methods, declared that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path, and that one who commits sexual misconduct is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
When that bhikṣuṇī exhorted this bhikṣuṇī, she stubbornly clung to her position and would not relinquish it.
That bhikṣuṇī is to be admonished up to three times to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it by the time of the third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that such a person has not performed the formal act (karmavācanā) and does not abandon such evil and heterodox views, should nevertheless keep them as a companion—performing the same formal acts (samānakarman) with them or staying in the same lodging (samānaśayanāsana)—it is a pāyattika.”
"If a śrāmaṇerikā should speak thus:
'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path,' that bhikṣuṇī should admonish this śrāmaṇerikā, saying:"
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. Slandering the World-Honored One is unwholesome, for the World-Honored One would never say such a thing, novice nun!"
"The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught that sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path, and that one who commits sexual misconduct is obstructed by that dharma.
When that bhikṣuṇī exhorted this śrāmaṇerī, she stubbornly persisted and would not relinquish her position.
That bhikṣuṇī should be formally admonished up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it during the course of the three admonitions, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should say to the śrāmaṇerikā:
"From this day forward, you are no longer a disciple of the Buddha.
You may not follow other bhikṣuṇīs; whereas other śrāmaṇerīs are permitted to stay with bhikṣuṇīs for two nights, you now have no such privilege."
Get out! Be gone!
You need not stay here.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been thus expelled, should keep her as a disciple or dwell together with her, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when being admonished in accordance with the Dharma, speaks as follows:
'I will not train in these precepts now; I shall wait until I have questioned those who are wise and uphold the Vinaya, and then I will raise my objections.'"
[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
If one seeks to understand [the meaning], one should pose difficult questions.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of reciting the precepts, speaks thus:"
"Sister! What is the use of these trivial precepts?
When these precepts are recited, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt."
Because she has disparaged the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of reciting the precepts, speaks these words:
'Sisters!'"
‘Only now do I know that this precept has come down as part of the Sūtra of Precepts, recited every half-month.
If other bhikṣuṇīs knew that this bhikṣuṇī had sat through two or three recitations of the precepts, let alone more.

That bhikṣuṇī was ignorant and lacked understanding; if she has committed an offense, she should be dealt with according to the Dharma, and furthermore, the rule regarding ignorance should be applied to her more strictly:
"Sister! You have gained no benefit and have acquired what is unwholesome."
"When you were reciting the precepts, you did not apply your mind, nor did you listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus.
Because she was ignorant of this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, after having participated in a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), later speaks as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of favoritism toward those she is close to, gives property belonging to the Saṃgha to them,
it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī,
when the Saṃgha is engaged in formal business, rises and leaves without having given her consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having already given her consent (*chanda*), later reproves [the matter], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, after two bhikṣuṇīs have been quarreling, listens to these words with the intent to report them to the other party, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes a bhikṣuṇī with her hand, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king—anointed by water—while the king has not yet emerged and the treasures have not yet been stored away, and she crosses the threshold, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of, or causes another to take hold of, precious objects or ornaments made of precious materials—except within a monastery or a lodging—this is a pāyattika."

Whether in a monastery or at a lodging place, if there is treasure or articles adorned with treasure, whether one takes hold of them oneself or instructs another to take hold of them—if it is something recognized [as belonging to someone], one should take it; such is the cause and condition, and nothing else.
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Buddha’s measure, except for the portion inserted into the mortise holes."
If she has finished cutting it and it exceeds [the prescribed length], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes cotton-wool (*tūla*) and uses it to make a rope bed, a wooden bed, a sleeping mat, or a sitting mat, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair of the three areas, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs the purification with water, it should be limited to two finger-joints each.
If she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a male organ out of lac, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī slaps another [bhikṣuṇī], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when a bhikṣu is not ill, provides him with water or fans him with a fan, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī begs for raw grain, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī disposes of excrement or urine in a vessel at night and does not look outside the wall before discarding it during the day, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī goes to watch performances or music, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village and stands or converses with a man in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a screened or concealed place together with a man, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having entered the lanes and alleys within a village, sends her companion far away and stands in a secluded place whispering with a man, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and sits down, and then departs without informing the host, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and sits upon a bed or seat without informing the host, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson's house and, without informing the host, spreads out a seat for herself and stays overnight, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dark room together with a man, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having carefully and accurately received her teacher’s words, speaks them to others, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, on account of a minor matter, utters a curse:
'May you fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma,' [it is a pāyattika]."
If I were to have such faults, I would fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma;
if you were to have such faults, you too would fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma.
"An *pāyattika*:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having engaged in a quarrel, does not properly remember the matter of the dispute and beats her breast and weeps, it is an *pāyattika*.'"
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lies down on the same bed with another, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same mat and under the same blanket with another, except at other times, it is a pāyattika.”

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has been resident there first and she arrived later, or knowing that she arrived first and the other is a resident, for the sake of causing annoyance, recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or gives instruction before her, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not attend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī with whom she lives who is ill, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, during the rains retreat, first permits another bhikṣuṇī to place a bed in her room, and later, out of anger, drives her out, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī wanders among the people at all times—during spring, summer, or winter—except for other valid reasons, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer rains retreat, does not depart, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels among the human settlements in a border region that is suspicious or dangerous, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels among the human settlements within a boundary that is suspicious or dangerous, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī associates with laymen or the sons of laymen, living with them and engaging in improper conduct,
and other bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'Sister!'"
"Do not associate with householders or the sons of householders, nor dwell with them, performing conduct that is discordant.
Sister! You should dwell separately."
"If one lives separately, there will be an increase in the dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha's Dharma.
When that bhikṣuṇī exhorted this bhikṣuṇī, she stubbornly clung to her position and would not relinquish it.
That bhikṣuṇī should be admonished three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
Up to the third admonition, it is well if she relinquishes it;
if she does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to visit a royal palace, a decorated painted hall, a garden, or a bathing pool, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī bathes in river water, spring water, flowing water, or pond water with her body exposed, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bathing robe, she should make it according to the prescribed measurement.
As for making it according to the measurement: it should be six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width."
If she exceeds [this limit], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sews a saṃghāṭī and exceeds five days, except when an emergency has arisen, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not inspect her saṃghāṭī for more than five days, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī creates an obstacle to the distribution of robes to the community of monks, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī puts on another's robe without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives a śramaṇa’s robe to an outsider or a layperson, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī forms this thought:
'The Saṃgha is distributing robes according to the Dharma; I shall obstruct it so that they do not distribute them, fearing that my disciples will not receive any.'"
...this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī forms such an intention:
'I shall cause the Saṃgha not to extend the *kaṭhina* robe now, but to extend it later, so that the five privileges may be relinquished for a long time'..."
“An *pāyattika*. ‘If a bhikṣuṇī, with such an intention as this:
“I shall obstruct the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha from releasing the kaṭhina robe, desiring that they remain deprived of the five privileges for a long time,” [commits such an act, it is an offense].’”
"An *pāyattika*.
'If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"Settle this dispute for me."'"
If she does not employ a skillful means to have it extinguished, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hands, gives food to a layperson or to a follower of an external sect, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a messenger for a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread with her own hands, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having entered the interior of a layperson's house, sits or lies down upon a small bed or a large bed, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson and asks the host to prepare a seat for her to stay overnight, yet departs the following day without taking leave of the host, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī recites or practices worldly incantations, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches others to recite or practice incantations, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is pregnant, ordains her and grants her full admission, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has an infant at her breast, grants her full admission, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon one who is less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a girl of eighteen years who has not completed two years of training in the precepts, even though she has reached twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to an eighteen-year-old girl who has completed two years of training in the precepts but has not been granted the six rules, once she has reached twenty."
Pāyattika:

"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon an eighteen-year-old girl who has completed two years of training in the precepts and the six rules, and who is twenty years of age, without the consent of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika offense."

"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who has previously been married and is ten years of age, she shall grant her two years of training in the precepts; when she has reached twelve years of age, she is permitted to receive full ordination."
If one bestows full ordination upon someone less than twelve years of age, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains another woman who was married at a young age and has completed two years of training in the precepts, yet, when she has reached the age of twelve, does not inform the Saṃgha before bestowing full ordination upon her, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon such a person, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains many disciples but does not instruct them in the training rules for two years, nor takes care of them with the two dharmas, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī does not follow her preceptor nun for two years, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon someone without the Sangha’s permission, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon another person when she herself is less than twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is twelve years of age or older confers full ordination upon another person without the consent of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha has not authorized her to confer full ordination upon another, should say:
'The Saṃgha possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion;
those who wish to authorize it shall do so, and those who do not wish to authorize it shall not.'"
“An *pāyattika*.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a woman whose father, mother, or husband has not given permission, it is an *pāyattika*.’”

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has been made sorrowful and angry by a young man or a man with whom she shared mutual affection, should ordain her and grant her full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā:
'Sister!'"
"Abandon this and learn that; we shall then grant you full ordination.
If she does not skillfully grant the full ordination, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā:"
"If you bring your robe and give it to me,
I shall grant you full ordination," he says;
yet, without employing the proper means to grant the full ordination, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another person before a year has passed [since her own ordination], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having conferred full ordination upon another person, does not go among the community of bhikṣus to confer full ordination until after one night has elapsed, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, does not go to receive instruction, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī, every half-month, should go among the community of bhikṣus to seek instruction."
If she does not seek [to do so], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat with the Saṃgha, should go before the bhikṣu-saṃgha and perform the *pravāraṇā* regarding three matters:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected."
If she does not do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī observes the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where no bhikṣus are present, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a bhikṣu monastery (*saṃghārāma*), enters without having announced her presence, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and does not properly remember the matter of the dispute, and later, out of anger and displeasure, reviles the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī has a boil or various kinds of sores on her body, and without informing the community or others, she should not have a man break them open or bandage them; this is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having previously accepted an invitation and having finished her meal, subsequently eats boiled rice, parched grain, cooked rice, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī harbors a mind of jealousy toward a household, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī anoints or rubs her body with fragrant substances, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī smears sesame dregs upon her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes another bhikṣuṇī to smear sesame dregs upon her body, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śikṣamāṇā to rub her body, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śrāmaṇerī to rub her body, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī causes a laywoman to anoint or massage her body, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī wears a garment with gathered folds at the knees, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī keeps articles for adorning a woman’s body, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī walks while wearing leather sandals and carrying a parasol, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, travels by means of a vehicle, except for a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village without wearing a saṃkakṣikā, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson at twilight without having been previously invited, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī opens the gate of the saṃghārāma at twilight and departs without having entrusted herself to another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī opens the gate of a saṃghārāma after sunset and goes out without having entrusted her affairs [to another], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī neither observes the earlier retreat nor the later retreat, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman constantly leaks urine and feces and constantly discharges nasal mucus and saliva, confers full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon a person with both sexual organs, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon one whose two channels are conjoined, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is the obstacle of debt or the obstacle of illness, confers full ordination [upon such a person], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī learns worldly arts and crafts to support her own life, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches worldly arts and crafts to a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has been expelled does not depart, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to ask a bhikṣu about the meaning [of the Dharma], yet asks without first seeking permission, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that one has arrived later while the other was already established there, and the other has arrived later while she was already established there, and desiring to vex the other, walks up and down, stands, sits, or lies down before them, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly builds a stūpa within a bhikṣu-saṃghārāma, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sees a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to meet him, pay him respect, prostrate to him, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit."
If she does not [desist], except for a specific cause, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of appearance, sways her body while walking, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī adorns herself like a woman, applying perfumes and rubbing them onto her body, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī causes a female non-Buddhist to apply perfumes and rub them onto her body, it is a pāyattika.”
"Sisters! I have already recited the one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the sisters:"
"Is there purity in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Sisters, since you are silent, there is purity in this matter."
This matter is to be held thus:
"Sisters, these eight *pātideśanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, begs for ghee to eat, she commits an offense that requires confession and is subject to censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, begs for oil as food, she commits an offense requiring confession and censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I should not have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method for repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, begs for honey-food, she commits an offense requiring confession and censure.
She should speak thus to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess it to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, begs for black stone-honey (kṛṣṇa-phāṇita) as food, she commits an offense requiring confession and censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess it before you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, begs for milk as food, she commits an offense requiring confession and censure.
She should speak thus to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method for repentance.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, begs for curd as food, she commits an offense of a nature requiring confession and censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying:
‘Sister! [I have committed an offense.]’”
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, begs for fish to eat, she commits an offense requiring confession and censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, begs for meat to eat, she commits an offense that requires confession and censure.
She should speak thus to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Sister!'"
"I have committed a censurable offense, which I ought not to have done.
I now confess this to you, Venerable Sister.
This is called the method of repentance.
"Sisters! I have already recited the eight *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas.
Now I ask the sisters: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
"Is there purity in this matter?
Thus it is asked up to three times. "Sisters!..."
In this matter, we are pure, because we remain silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
"Sisters!..."
These rules of training for the community are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of Precepts:
"One should train oneself to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) properly."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe tucked back over one shoulder.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe tucked back over one shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit in the house of a layperson with my robe wrapped around my neck.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit in the house of a layperson with one's head covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson by jumping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not skip over steps when entering the house of a layperson to sit.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not squat while inside the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson with my hands on my hips.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson with hands on my hips while seated.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson shaking my body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson while swaying the body and sit down.
One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson while dangling the arms.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson with arms flung out while seated.
One should train oneself: 'One must enter the house of a layperson well-covered.
One should train oneself: 'One must enter the house of a layperson and sit down well-covered.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not walk into the house of a layperson while looking left and right.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit in the house of a layperson while walking in and looking left and right.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the homes of laypeople in silence.
One should train oneself: 'I shall sit in the homes of laypeople in silence.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the homes of laypeople while walking about in jest or laughter.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter the house of a layperson or sit there while laughing or joking.
One should train oneself: 'One must receive food with mindfulness.
One should train oneself: 'One must receive food with a level alms bowl.'"
"One should train oneself to receive the soup with a level bowl.
One should train oneself to eat the soup and rice in equal proportions.
One should train oneself to eat in proper sequence."
"One should train oneself: 'One must not pick at food from within the bowl while eating.
One should train oneself: 'If a bhikṣuṇī is not ill, she must not seek out soup or rice for her own sake.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.
One should train oneself: 'One must not look into the bowl of the person sitting beside one while they are eating.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When eating, one should maintain the mindfulness of the bowl.
One should train oneself: 'One must not take large mouthfuls of rice.
One should train oneself: 'One must not open the mouth wide in anticipation of food.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not speak with food in the mouth.
One should train oneself: 'One must not clump food together and toss it into the mouth from a distance.
One should train oneself: 'One must not let food fall and scatter.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat with the cheeks puffed out.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat making a chewing sound.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not take large mouthfuls of food.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not lick the food with the tongue.
One should train oneself: 'One must not shake the hands while eating.
One should train oneself: 'One must not eat by grasping at scattered grains of rice with the hand.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not hold a drinking vessel with soiled hands.
One should train oneself: 'One must not discard water used for washing the alms-bowl inside a layperson's house.
One should train oneself: 'One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon living grass or leaves, except in cases of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not void excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva into pure water.
One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not stand while voiding excrement or urine.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their robe draped over one shoulder in a disrespectful manner, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one whose neck is wrapped with a robe, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their head covered, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their head wrapped, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has their hands on their hips, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, one must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, one must not preach the Dharma to those riding on vehicles.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not stay overnight in a stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not conceal wealth or goods within a stūpa, except for the purpose of securing them.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a Buddhist stūpa wearing leather sandals.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in my hand.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk around a stūpa wearing leather sandals.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a stūpa wearing boots.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather footwear in one's hands.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit and eat beneath a stūpa, leaving grass or food that defiles the ground.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'One must not bury a corpse at the base of a stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'One must not cremate a corpse at the base of a stūpa.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not burn a corpse toward a Buddha-stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'One must not burn a corpse within four paces of a Buddha-stūpa, so as not to allow its foul odor to enter.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not pass beneath a stūpa carrying a corpse's garment or a bed, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed.
One should train oneself: 'One must not defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha-stūpa.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not defecate or urinate toward a stūpa of the Buddha.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not defecate or urinate around the four sides of a stūpa of the Buddha, causing foul odors to enter.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not chew tooth-sticks beneath a stupa of the Buddha.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not chew tooth-sticks while facing a Buddha stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not chew tooth-sticks within four paces of a Buddha stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not spit or sneeze beneath a Buddha stūpa.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not spit toward a stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'One must not spit within four paces of a stūpa.
One should train oneself: 'One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not occupy an upper room while placing a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room.
One should train oneself: 'If another person is seated and I am standing, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one must not preach the Dharma to someone who is lying down while one is sitting.
One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one must not preach the Dharma to someone who is seated while one is not seated."
"One should train oneself: when another person is seated on a high seat and one is seated on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: when another person is in front and one is behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
"One should train oneself: if another person is on a high walking path and one is on a lower walking path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: if another person is on the path and one is off the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
